edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Χρὴ οὖν ζητεῖν τὸ ἁρμοζόντως τῷ λογικῷ καὶ ἡμέρῳ ζῴῳ καὶ λελογισμένως πάντα πράττοντι βρωτὸν καὶ οὐ βρωτὸν. καὶ μὴ κατὰ ἀποκλήρωσιν σέβειν ὄϊς ἢ αἶγας ἢ τὰς θηλείας βοῦς. καὶ τούτων μὲν ἀπέχεσθαι μέτριον, πολὺ γὰρ χρήσιμον ἀπὸ τούτων τῶν ζῴων ἀνθρώποις γίνεται· τὸ δὲ καὶ κροκοδείλων φείδεσθαι, καὶ εἶναι ἱεροὺς αὐτοὺς οὐκ οἶδα τίνος μυθολογουμένου θεοῦ, πῶς οὐκ ἔστι πάντων ἠλιθιώτατον; σφόδρα γὰρ ἐμβροντήτων ἐστὶ τὸ φείδεσθαι ζῴων οὐ φειδομένων καὶ περιέπειν ζῷα ἀνθρώπους καταθοινώμενα. ἀλλὰ Κέλσῳ ἀρέσκουσι μὲν οἱ κατά τινα πάτρια κροκοδείλους σέβοντες καὶ περιέποντες, καὶ οὐδεὶς λόγος κατ᾿ ἐκείνων αὐτῷ γέγραπται· ψεκτοὶ δ᾿ εἶναι φαίνονται Χριστιανοὶ, τὴν κακίαν βδελύσσεσθαι διδασκόμενοι καὶ τὰ ἀπὸ κακίας ἔργα ἐκτρέπεσθαι, τὴν δ᾿ ἀρετὴν σέβειν καὶ τιμᾶν ὡς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ γεγενημένην καὶ οὖσαν υἱὸν θεοῦ. οὐ γὰρ παρὰ τὸ θηλυκὸν ὄνομα καὶ τῇ οὐσίᾳ θήλειαν νομιστέον εἶναι τὴν σοφίαν καὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην, ἅπερ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, ὡς ὁ γνήσιος αὐτοῦ μαθητὴς παρέστησε λέγων περὶ αὐτοῦ· „ὃς ἐγενήθη σοφία ἡμῖν ἀπὸ θεοῦ δικαιοσύνη τε καὶ ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις.“ κἂν δεύτερον οὖν λέγωμεν θεὸν, ἴστωσαν ὅτι τὸν δεύτερον θεὸν οὐκ ἄλλο τι λέγομεν ἢ τὴν περιεκτικὴν πασῶν ἀρετῶν ἀρετὴν καὶ τὸν περιεκτικὸν παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν λόγου τῶν κατὰ φύσιν καὶ προηγουμένως γεγενημένων καὶ εἰς χρήσιμον τοῦ παντὸς λόγον· ὅντινα τῇ Ἰησοῦ μάλιστα παρὰ πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ᾠκειῶσθαι καὶ ἡνῶσθαί φαμεν, μόνου τελείως χωρῆσαι δεδυνημένου τὴν ἄκραν μετοχὴν τοῦ αὐτολόγου καὶ τῆς αὐτοσοφίας καὶ τῆς αὐτοδικαιοσύνης.
thought_title: Crocodiles, virtue and the second God
pass_a_gloss: It is necessary therefore to seek what is edible and not edible fittingly for the rational and tame/gentle living being that does all things reasoningly, and not according to allotment/at random to revere sheep or goats or the female cattle. And to abstain from these is moderate, for much useful comes to humans from these animals; but also to spare crocodiles, and that they are sacred of I-know-not-which mythologised god, how is it not of all things most foolish? For it is very much of thunderstruck/senseless people to spare animals not sparing and to tend/cherish animals feasting on humans. But to Celsus are pleasing those who according to some ancestral ways revere and tend crocodiles, and no word against them has been written by him; but blameworthy the Christians appear, being taught to loathe vice and to turn away from the works from vice, and to revere and honour virtue as begotten by God and being Son of God. For not because of the feminine name must one think wisdom and righteousness to be female also in essence, which according to us is the Son of God, as his genuine disciple showed, saying about him: 'who became wisdom for us from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption.' Even if then we say a second god, let them know that by the second god we say nothing other than the virtue comprehensive of all virtues, and the Word/reason comprehensive of every whatsoever reason/principle of the things made according to nature and primarily/by first intent and for the use of the whole, [the] Word; which [Word] we say has been appropriated and united to the [soul] of Jesus most of all beyond every soul, he alone having been able to contain/receive perfectly the highest participation of the Word-itself and Wisdom-itself and Righteousness-itself.

pass_b_english: We must therefore inquire what is fit to be eaten and what is not, in a way that befits a rational and gentle living being that does everything by reason, and not worship sheep or goats or cows arbitrarily. To abstain from these is within reason, for much that is useful comes to human beings from these animals. But to spare even crocodiles, and to hold them sacred to some mythical god, I know not which, how is this not the most foolish thing of all? For it is the mark of people quite out of their senses to spare animals that do not spare, and to cherish animals that feast on human beings.

Yet Celsus is pleased with those who worship and cherish crocodiles according to some ancestral custom, and he has not written a single word against them. It is the Christians who seem to him to deserve blame, though they are taught to loathe vice and to turn away from the works that come from vice, and to revere and honour virtue as begotten by God and as being the Son of God. For we must not suppose that wisdom and righteousness are female in their essence because their names are feminine; and in our teaching these are the Son of God, as his genuine disciple made plain when he said of him: “who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

So even if we speak of a second God, let them know that by the second God we mean nothing other than the virtue that contains all virtues, and the Word that contains every rational principle whatever of the things that have come into being according to nature, by primary intent, and for the benefit of the whole. This Word, we say, has been joined to the soul of Jesus as its own and united with it, more closely than with any other soul, since he alone was able to receive perfectly the highest share in the very Word, the very Wisdom and the very Righteousness.
notes: κατὰ ἀποκλήρωσιν ('by allotment') = arbitrarily, as chance assigns, i.e. each nation worshipping whatever animal its custom fell upon; rendered 'as the lot happens to fall'. ἐμβρόντητος ('thunderstruck') = senseless; rendered 'quite out of their senses'. The feminine-noun remark answers the possible objection that Christians, revering ἀρετή/σοφία/δικαιοσύνη (feminine nouns), worship a female power like the goddesses Celsus lists in 5.37-38; the antecedent of ἅπερ (neuter plural) is wisdom and righteousness, and the verb ἐστιν is singular ('which is the Son of God'). 'δεύτερον θεόν' kept as 'a second God', capitalised because Origen means the Son. The λόγος wordplay (the Word containing every λόγος of created things) is kept as 'Word' / 'rational principle'; reviewer: the final λόγον is the head noun of τὸν περιεκτικόν ('the Word that contains ...'), and εἰς χρήσιμον τοῦ παντός goes with γεγενημένων ('made ... for the benefit of the whole'); rendered so. ᾠκειῶσθαι ('made his own, appropriated') and ἡνῶσθαι ('united') rendered as two verbs. γεγενημένην (single ν, from γίνομαι) said of virtue/the Son is kept as 'begotten', since the clause names it the Son of God and the single/double ν spellings are confused in the manuscripts. τῇ Ἰησοῦ supplies ψυχῇ from παρὰ πᾶσαν ψυχήν. αὐτόλογος, αὐτοσοφία, αὐτοδικαιοσύνη rendered 'the very Word, the very Wisdom and the very Righteousness'. 1 Corinthians 1:30 matches the Greek closely (ὃς ἐγενήθη σοφία ἡμῖν ἀπὸ θεοῦ, δικαιοσύνη τε καὶ ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις).
